items.title: Remarkable Observatory Receives Orbital Radio
items.summary: There’s nothing quite so nostalgic as the time honored tradition of tuning across the HF bands, picking out signals from the noise. Add satellites and VHF/UHF to the mix, then replace the old shortwave receiver with a smattering of software-defined radios. With an ESP32 controlled antenna switch (and the matching antennae), some Python, and a dash of Claude Code, and you’re approaching what [Tommy Lather] has done with his Starlab Observatory . Determined to find out what was inhabiting his local electromagnetic spectrum, [Tommy] picked up a cheap RTL-SDR receiver and an antenna. The goal? Receiving some ISS image transmissions. The results? Let’s say mixed . But it lit a fire, and soon, he had more hardware than he could handle on his own. The slope became slippery, and before he knew it, the Starlab Observatory was an Open Source GitHub Project ! What makes it an Observatory instead of a random menagerie of radio memorabilia? Intelligence. An ESP32 based antenna switch takes commands from a dedicated Ubuntu computer. The PC, running Starlab , predicts satellite passes, and selects the correct receiver and antenna combination to receive data, which then gets logged and processed. Multiple jobs can run at once. The RF spectrum doesn’t stand a chance! We have to wonder if a fully programmable az-el mount such as the AntRunner isn’t in [Tommy]’s near future! items.title: Linux in a Browser Tab
items.summary: Linux was once distributed on CDs and DVDs stuck to the front of computer magazines. Now, technology has advanced to the point where you can simply run a Linux kernel right in your browser. That’s precisely what you get with Unkernel from [pithings]. Unkernel is described as “Linux 7.x built as a single wasm module with an MMU.” Yes, thanks to the magic of WebAssembly, you can run Linux in a browser tab at a decent fraction of native speed. All the proper kernel stuff—like syscalls, the scheduler, memory management, file systems, and networking—is compiled code. User programs are then emulated with a just-in-time compiler, so you can run Ubuntu and Alpine packages without any fuss. You get a shell, package manager, persistent storage, sound, and internet access out of the box. It’s basically a whole Linux computer sitting in a single browser tab for your convenience. It’s generally not as fast as running the kernel natively, but where you need a little Linux on the go, it should come in clutch. items.title: A Pen Plotter to Draw You Up (on) the Wall
items.summary: Back in our day you were told not to draw on the walls; nowadays we have robots for that– like Mural 2.0 by [Nik Ivanov]. If the name doesn’t give it away, this is a large format pen plotter made to draw, well, murals. It’s also not [Nik]’s first rodeo, though this version seems considerably improved from the orignial version. He’s now using a FluidNC board based on an ESP32 and TMC2209 stepper drivers, while the steppers they drive are a pair of NEMA 17 pancake units. Using pancakes for this application makes sense, as the steppers are on the machine and must pull themselves up against gravity using the single belt that is anchored at ceiling level. The kinematics of that mean you don’t get the full area between the anchor points– you lose 20% at the edges– but you can still get a pretty big mural going. In the demo/build video embedded below, it looks like you’re more limited by marker life, [Nik] cautioning that past about 500 m of line things can start to get a bit weak as the pen dries out. He’s working on a ‘pause and replace pen’ routine for the next firmware version to help with that project. For now, the WiFi-based interface [Nik] has on the ESP32 gives you that path length in advance, and can even process both SVG and raster images with both a sine-wave style squiggle and finite-curve style space filling. This isn’t the fastest pen plotter we’ve seen on these pages, and it might not quite be the simplest, either, but [Nik] has put together a very easy build that you could do with your nieces and nephews content in the knowledge that the easy-to-use firmware will let them keep making murals when you aren’t there– assuming, that is, that their mother lets them draw on the walls. items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases
